messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Ministry Worker
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 47

# The Weight of What He Carried Home

Marcus is twenty-one years old, newly married, and looks older than he should. There is a steadiness to the way he holds himself in the room — the kind that comes not from confidence but from years of practicing stillness in places where stillness kept you safe.

He spent eight months in a conflict zone in Eastern Europe as part of a humanitarian relief organization, distributing food, coordinating medical supply chains, and helping displaced families navigate registration systems. He had volunteered the summer after finishing secondary school, idealistic and capable, fluent in two languages, eager to be useful. What he encountered in those months reshaped him in ways he is only beginning to understand now that he is back home, working a desk job at the same social ministry organization that sent him, and sleeping beside his wife in a quiet apartment that sometimes feels like it belongs to someone else.

The worst of it happened during his fifth month in the field. His convoy was caught near a shelled residential area. He was not injured. He keeps saying that — *I wasn't injured* — as though it settles something. But he watched a colleague pulled from the vehicle with shrapnel wounds, held pressure on the wound for twenty-two minutes while artillery continued in the distance, and spent the following hours helping to document civilian casualties in a temporary triage site. He remembers the smell most of all. He says he cannot describe it without his body remembering it before his words do.

He returned home four months ago. His wife, Lena, noticed the changes before he could name them himself. He stopped sleeping through the night almost immediately. He wakes between two and four in the morning, heart already racing, sometimes unsure where he is, reaching for the edge of the mattress to orient himself. The dreams are not always dramatic — sometimes it is just the smell, or the sound of something dropping, and he wakes drenched in sweat with a feeling he can only describe as *knowing something terrible is about to happen*.

During the day, he manages. He is good at managing. At work, he processes intake forms for asylum seekers, and he approaches the role with genuine care. But when a client describes crossing a border under fire, or when he encounters a photograph in a case file, something shifts in him that he cannot fully control. His chest tightens. His thinking narrows. He has learned to excuse himself to the bathroom, run cold water over his wrists, and return to his desk. His colleagues think he is thorough and composed. He has not told any of them what happened.

He avoids the news. He has muted every social media account that might post footage from conflict zones. He has declined two invitations to speak at organizational fundraisers about his field experience, telling himself he is not a good public speaker, which Lena knows is not true.

What troubles him most, he says quietly, is the distance he feels from the person he was before. He married Lena six weeks after returning — the wedding had been planned before he left — and he describes their relationship with real warmth. But he feels like he is watching their life together from slightly outside of it, present in all the practical ways and somehow not quite there. He loves her. He is certain of that. He just cannot always feel it the way he thinks he should.

He came to therapy because Lena asked him to, and because one morning he sat in his car outside the office for forty minutes, unable to go in, and that frightened him enough to finally make the call. He is articulate, self-aware, and deeply reluctant to believe that what happened to him counts as something serious. *Other people had it so much worse,* he says. He says it the way people do when they are hoping someone will finally disagree with them.
